extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated general readers interested in human evolution and variation
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter material outlining the principal phenomena and proposed causes of physical and mental variability in humans, and how these laws of variation compare with those in other animals. It collects empirical examples and articulates a set of 'laws' or headings used to analyze variation and inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of body and mind in man
rubrics_metrics.description: It is manifest that man is now subject to much variability. No two individuals of the same race are quite alike. There is an equally great amount of diversity in the proportions and dimensions of the various parts of the body; the length of the legs being one of the most variable points. The variability or diversity of the mental faculties in men of the same race ... is so notorious that not a word need here be said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by numerous empirical observations: differences in skull shape between regions, diversity in teeth and muscles, arterial courses, and mental dispositions observed in captive and wild animals. References to large-scale measurements (e.g. US soldiers) and anatomical surveys are given to quantify variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater number of facts have been collected with respect to the transmission of the most trifling, as well as of the most important characters in man, than in any of the lower animals. So in regard to mental qualities, their transmission is manifest in our dogs, horses, and other domestic animals. With man we see similar facts in almost every family; and we now know ... that genius ... tends to be inherited; and, on the other hand, it is too certain that insanity and deteriorated mental powers likewise run in families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats inheritance as a central principle: physical and mental traits can be transmitted across generations. Cites Galton and many family-based observations; uses inheritance as a basis to argue that variation may accumulate and be acted on by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of variability
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to the causes of variability, we are in all cases very ignorant; but we can see that in man as in the lower animals, they stand in some relation to the conditions to which each species has been exposed, during several generations. Domesticated animals vary more than those in a state of nature; and this is apparently due to the diversified and changing nature of the conditions to which they have been subjected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasises both ignorance and observed correlations: variation tends to be greater under diversified/changing conditions (e.g. domestication, wide geographic ranges), and different occupations/grades in society correlate with morphological differences. Examples: measurements of soldiers vs sailors; differences among Polynesian classes. Cautions that precise causal mechanisms are often unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of variation apply equally to man and lower animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only does variability appear to be induced in man and the lower animals by the same general causes, but in both the same parts of the body are affected in a closely analogous manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin refers to Godron, Quatrefages, and Geoffroy St.-Hilaire for detailed demonstrations. He uses this parity to justify applying principles found in domestic animals and wild species to human variation and anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and definite action of changed conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct and definite action of changed conditions, as exhibited by all or nearly all the individuals of the same species, varying in the same manner under the same circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats this as a distinct heading among the laws of variation. He presents empirical examples (e.g. stature differences among men born/reared in different US states; sailors' growth patterns) showing local influences on stature and body proportions. He also notes cases where expected environmental effects (climate, soil) do not clearly explain observed differences, and stresses the difficulty of deriving precise causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of the increased use and disuse of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strengthens the muscles in the individual, and complete disuse ... weakens them. When the eye is destroyed, the optic nerve often becomes atrophied. Bones increase not only in thickness, but in length, from carrying a greater weight. Different occupations, habitually followed, lead to changed proportions in various parts of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sailors with relatively longer legs and shorter arms, muscular changes from habitual activity, and thicker skin on the soles of infants inherited from ancestral pressure. Darwin treats it as plausible that such acquired modifications might become hereditary over many generations, and uses examples (Rengger, Cranz) to suggest cultural/occupational effects across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrests of development (paedomorphic/arrested structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrested development: parts in the former state continue to grow whilst still retaining their early condition. Various monstrosities come under this head; and some, as a cleft palate, are known to be occasionally inherited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives the arrested brain-development of microcephalous idiots as an example: skulls smaller, simpler cerebral convolutions, prognathous jaws, brute-like behaviour and instincts, and other characters resembling lower types. He uses such cases to argue how arrested development can resemble ancestral adult forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion (atavism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a structure is arrested in its development, but still continues growing, until it closely resembles a corresponding structure in some lower and adult member of the same group, it may in one sense be considered as a case of reversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats reversion as the reappearance of long-lost characters and notes that arrested development may produce structures resembling ancestral adult forms (e.g. the simple brain of a microcephalous idiot resembling an ape). Reversion is presented as one of the laws/principles explaining some anomalous traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of homologous parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The cohesion of homologous parts (one of the heads under which Darwin arranges laws of variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as an organizing principle: homologous parts tend to vary together or exhibit linked modification. Darwin refers readers to his fuller treatments elsewhere; in this chapter it is listed among the principal categories for analyzing variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of multiple parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The variability of multiple parts (another heading in Darwin's list of laws of variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means that when structures are repeated or multiple (e.g. digits, teeth), they often vary together or show characteristic patterns of variation. Cited as a general law applicable to man and other animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation of growth; but of this law I have found no good instance in the case of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists this as a putative law (where increased growth of one part is compensated by decreased growth elsewhere) but notes lack of clear examples in humans; still includes it among the conceptual tools for understanding variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of mechanical pressure of one part on another
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of the mechanical pressure of one part on another; as of the pelvis on the cranium of the infant in the womb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites mechanical developmental interactions (e.g. pelvic constraints affecting fetal skull shape) as a mechanism producing variation and potential inheritance of altered forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlated variation (listed among the principal causes/laws), meaning changes in one part producing changes in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes that many characters do not vary independently but in correlated suites; he uses these correlations to explain secondary or linked changes (e.g. extremity development correlated with jaw development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Widely-ranging species are more variable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a well-known law that widely-ranging species are much more variable than species with restricted ranges; and the variability of man may with more truth be compared with that of widely-ranging species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses human examples (Americans, Polynesians) to show large internal variation correlated with wide geographic ranges; he argues this supports comparing human variability to that of widely-ranging animal species rather than to strictly domesticated forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited role of deliberate human breeding (selection) historically
rubrics_metrics.description: In another and much more important respect, man differs widely from any strictly domesticated animal; for his breeding has never long been controlled, either by methodical or unconscious selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes exceptions (Prussian grenadiers, Spartan infanticide and selection) but emphasizes that, broadly, human mating/breeding has not been subject to the kind of sustained artificial selection that shapes domestic breeds; nevertheless sexual selection and unconscious selection (social pressures) have affected some traits.
